packages.title: A Little Winter for Sale
packages.prompt_text:
# Prompt contract

## Verbatim writing prompt

> **[WP] As a traveler, you've been exploring the desert for days, before coming upon a city so far from water, nestled against a mountainside. You find that in the mountains cave, is an ice dragon far from home, enjoying being paid to simply sell small bouts of it's power**

## Story controls

- Working title: A Little Winter for Sale
- Target length: 2,500–4,000 words
- POV: First-person traveler, with the ice dragon's agency made legible through
  direct interaction rather than an omniscient explanation.
- Tense: Past.
- Tone and genre: Wonder-forward secondary-world fantasy with dry humor,
  tactile desert imagery, and grounded civic/economic stakes.
- Audience/content rating: Teen / PG; dehydration risk and non-graphic danger,
  no explicit sexual content or graphic violence.
- Required elements: A traveler has spent days exploring a desert; an
  apparently impossible city stands far from surface water against a mountain;
  a mountain cave houses an ice dragon far from its homeland; the dragon is
  knowingly paid and genuinely enjoys selling small, bounded uses of its cold;
  the city's relationship to those transactions matters to the plot; the
  traveler's discovery produces a consequential choice and a resolved ending.
- Prohibited elements: Do not make the dragon secretly enslaved, coerced, or
  awaiting rescue; do not erase the prompt's pleasure-in-payment premise; do not
  make the dragon's power infinite or costless; do not reduce the city to a
  static twist with no human or dragon stakes; do not contradict established
  shared-universe canon.

## Assumptions

- The city, mountain, traveler, and ice dragon may be local inventions unless
  canon research finds a relevant established identity or location.
- "Small bouts" means brief, metered applications of cold whose cumulative
  limits and pricing can create meaningful choices without making the bargain
  abusive.
- "Far from home" implies voluntary travel or migration and homesickness, not
  captivity; the dragon can enjoy its present work while still missing home.
- The city's distance from water should be made materially plausible through
  storage, condensation, ice, hidden geology, trade, or a combination rather
  than handwaved.
- The story may examine fair exchange, civic dependence, and hospitality, but
  it should keep its sense of delight and avoid turning into a policy lecture.

## Completion tests

- The result is a complete short story, not a synopsis or chapter fragment.
- The central promise of the prompt is dramatized and resolved.
- The dragon is an active character with a clear reason to enjoy the work and a
  credible ability to accept, refuse, and price each use of power.
- The city's water system and the dragon's bounded contribution are concrete
  enough that the reader understands both the marvel and its limits.
- The traveler makes or enables a choice that changes the immediate situation;
  the ending pays off the dragon's distance from home and the meaning of fair
  payment.
- The story passes canon and continuity review.
- Every character-facing name and alias is checked against `stories/NAMES.md`;
  any deliberate reuse has a documented narrative reason.

packages.prompt_text:
# Prompt contract

## Verbatim writing prompt

> **[WP] Introducing a boyfriend or girlfriend to the family can be either very pleasant or very stressful. When you come from a lineage of necromancers, these feelings are amplified, as relatives who died decades ago might show up for a visit.**

## Story controls

- Working title: A Place for the Living
- Target length: 3,000–3,800 words
- POV: Close third person, centered on the living partner entering the family
- Tense: Past
- Tone and genre: Warm dark comedy with gothic domestic fantasy, mounting social
  pressure, and an emotionally sincere ending
- Audience/content rating: Teen; death and the visible dead are present, but no
  graphic gore, sexual content, or cruelty
- Required elements: A serious romantic partner is introduced to a necromantic
  family; the meal begins plausibly pleasantly and becomes increasingly
  stressful; at least one relative dead for decades attends in an active,
  consequential role; the supernatural complications expose an ordinary
  relationship fear; the central family conflict reaches a decisive resolution
  during the visit
- Prohibited elements: No “all necromancers are evil” framing; no resolution
  based solely on a convenient spell failure or villain defeat; no treating
  deceased relatives as disposable joke props; no contradiction of established
  shared-universe rules

## Assumptions

- The lineage may practice a local, household-scale form of necromancy only if
  canon research finds room for it; its limits and costs must remain consistent
  with the shared universe.
- The visiting partner already knows the family practices necromancy, so the
  dramatic pressure comes from intimacy and family judgment rather than a
  prolonged hidden-magic reveal.
- The story will stand alone without requiring knowledge of other stories.
- Romantic gender will be chosen during planning after the name registry and
  canon brief are checked; the relationship will be affectionate and
  established enough that this introduction matters.

## Completion tests

- The result is a complete short story, not a synopsis or chapter fragment.
- A living partner meets the necromantic family in a sustained on-page visit,
  and a relative dead for decades materially changes the encounter.
- The ordinary emotional question—whether the partner has a place in this
  family—is answered by a costly choice, not merely by reassurance.
- The pleasant and stressful sides of the introduction both appear, with
  escalating social and supernatural complications.
- The story passes both draft and final canon/continuity review gates.
- Every character-facing name and alias is checked against `stories/NAMES.md`;
  any deliberate reuse has a documented narrative reason.

packages.title: All Accounts Due
packages.prompt_text:
# Prompt contract

> Contract status: REVISED AGAIN FOR COSMIC CLIMAX
> Story slug: `all-accounts-due`
> Captured: 2026-08-05

## Verbatim writing prompt

> [WP] You have no magic, but as you've helped others you've amassed tons of favors, artifacts, etc. Today everyone woke up to find thier max mana is zero.

## Story controls

- Working title: All Accounts Due
- Target length: 4,500–6,000 words, giving the culmination enough room while
  remaining a complete short story rather than a synopsis.
- POV: Chosen during planning for strongest dramatic effect.
- Tense: Chosen during planning for strongest dramatic effect.
- Structure: Frame the story at the already assembled extinction site, then let
  the body focus on six major quest/adventure flashbacks comprising roughly
  55–65% of the prose. Each flashback is triggered by a present relic, scar,
  opponent, or favor-holder and shows how the wholly nonmagical, non-superhuman
  protagonist survived, helped, bargained, stole, received, or earned the exact
  resource now required. The flashbacks need not be chronological, but together
  they must feel like the great adventures of a lifetime. The final 35–45%
  returns continuously to the present for the extended `No More Magic` climax
  and the goddess's immediate realization. Nothing follows her failed attempt
  to use the power Faris has ended.
- Tone and genre: World-ending event fantasy; epic, elegiac, cumulative, and
  mythic, cosmic, spectacular, and intimate enough that the scale is felt
  through irreversible personal losses.
- Audience/content rating: Teen.
- Required elements: A male protagonist who has never had magic and uses he/him
  pronouns; years of helping
  others that have yielded consequential favors, relationships, and artifacts;
  the permanent end of magic across the world; an entirely original cast,
  setting, history, magical systems, cultures, and kinds of life created for
  this story; visible collapse across those distinct systems; a lifetime of
  learning, helping, collecting consequential magical artifacts, and earning
  freely renewed favors that all converge in one cosmic action; and a climax in
  which the protagonist explicitly chooses or declares "No More Magic" and
  thereby makes the end permanent; followed immediately by the deceived
  goddess realizing what he did, trying to act, and finding that she cannot.
- Adventure-build requirements: multiple original quests with mythic variety;
  many relics obtained through a mix of collection, theft, bargains, rescues,
  and freely given gifts; and personal favors presently owed by original
  goddesses, demon lords, dragons, kings, and other powerful beings. These are
  new standalone identities, not reused characters or renamed analogues.
- Prohibited elements: No direct use of Marvel characters, settings, or plot;
  the *House of M* note controls the event's scale, culmination, and emotional
  premise only. Do not reuse, cameo, name, or directly reference any character
  from another repository story. Do not make this a crossover or import another
  story's named location, artifact, institution, magical system, crisis, title,
  or relationship as the source of grandeur. Do not reduce the event to one
  neighborhood emergency, restore magic by the ending, grant the protagonist
  hidden magic, or substitute a generic catastrophe montage for earned
  historical and personal consequence. Agriculture, water, seed, routes, and
  disaster logistics may appear as consequences, but they may not be the main
  objective, central spectacle, or climactic payoff. Do not add a dawn coda,
  explanation, forgiveness, reconstruction, or epilogue after the goddess's
  failed response.

## Assumptions

- The user's clarification is explicit authority to establish a world-wide,
  permanent end of magic in the story's present material world. It does not by
  itself erase magic from unrelated earlier eras, other timelines, afterlives,
  or planes unless current canon and the revised canon brief support that reach.
- The story is a wholly standalone culmination, not an isolated side incident
  and not a shared-cast event. Its sense of prior history must be established
  inside this story through the protagonist's own years of service, original
  relationships, original artifacts, and the visible institutions and cultural
  expectations that now end. Canon research may constrain chronology and world
  rules behind the scenes, but the prose may not borrow another story's named
  people, places, artifacts, systems, titles, or plot history.
- The protagonist and his allies intentionally cause the zero-capacity event
  at the climax. Present-time action begins before the declaration, while magic
  remains active and spectacular. The declaration wave extinguishes living
  capacity, stored power, structures, crossings, beings' active faculties, and
  every possible reserve together. The extinction wave itself must establish
  world-wide zero and permanence before the final goddess beat.
- Original artifacts may retain stored charge or useful nonmagical functions
  only if the story defines their bounded mechanisms; they do not become
  autonomous magic users, and no charge may leave magic surviving at the end.
- The protagonist's decisive advantage should come from earned trust,
  practical knowledge, and reciprocal obligations, not a concealed magical
  awakening.
- There is no restoration engine, restoration attempt, recovery quest, or
  relic-based offer to bring magic back. The story is not about fixing the
  opening zero event. It is about executing the lifetime plan that creates it.
  The final irreversible answer is "No More Magic."
- The protagonist's lifelong lack of magic may let him resist, enter, carry,
  witness, or decide where active users cannot, but it is not a concealed power,
  immunity, prophecy, or chosen destiny. His access to the climax must also
  depend on accumulated knowledge, specific artifacts, and freely renewed help.
- The protagonist is not secretly a master warrior, inventor, savant, or holder
  of another compensating superpower. His adventures succeed through nerve,
  persistence, empathy, bargains, observation, preparation, opportunism, and
  other ordinary abilities plausibly learned over a lifetime.
- The goddess freely gave and later armed the necessary relic, but Faris used a
  technically accurate narrow promise and intentionally withheld the world-wide
  scope. Her act is voluntary but not informed consent to extinction. The story
  must make the deception fair in retrospect and preserve her anger, betrayal,
  and moral claim rather than treating the twist as a joke or absolving Faris.
- The climax should make the cosmos-scale loss visible in-scene: magical skies,
  structures, beings, realms or crossings, and accumulated wonders end before
  the protagonist and the world. Reports may widen scale but cannot substitute
  for spectacle and decisive action.
- The principal cast and artifacts must already be converging when the framing
  present opens. The quests are dramatized as flashbacks rather than a new
  assembly journey. Do not administer the aftermath; the declaration is the
  climactic payoff to the adventures that form the body.

## Completion tests

- The result is a complete short story, not a synopsis or chapter fragment.
- The central promise of the prompt is dramatized and resolved.
- The end of magic is witnessed across multiple original systems and
  communities with immediate civilizational, ecological, political, spiritual,
  and identity consequences.
- The story feels like the payoff of years of accumulated relationships and
  artifacts, not an ordinary emergency with enlarged numbers.
- At least six materially different favors or relationships—including original

## Verbatim writing prompt

> **[WP] In a fantasy world much like our own, where magic has long since die out, the greatest wonder is a floating city that should not be possible. With over four million residents, it's ancient nuclear reactors are beginning to fail, and the results are catastrophic.**

## Story controls

- Working title: Four Million Falling
- Target length: 2,500–4,000 words
- POV: Close third person through one principal viewpoint.
- Tense: Past.
- Tone and genre: Urgent science-fantasy disaster drama with human-scale stakes
  inside a city-scale catastrophe.
- Audience/content rating: Teen / PG-13; peril and loss without graphic gore.
- Required elements: A fantasy society recognizably like our own; magic believed
  extinct for a long time; an apparently impossible ancient floating city with
  more than four million residents; failing nuclear reactors; catastrophic
  consequences dramatized on the page; a complete emotional and causal ending.

- "Catastrophic" requires irreversible loss and mass disruption, but does not
  require the extermination of all four million residents.

  and the story-specific plan.

  with restrained wit and a hopeful but costly resolution.

  threat and discussion of coerced marriage; no explicit sexual content.

  to one of the adult daughters of the King of the North; the northern king's
  brutality and reputed strength of ten men; a concrete need for the northern
  army; meaningful choice for the prospective bride; an alliance whose terms
  and cost are dramatized; a complete resolution.

  violence; romanticizing coercion or treating a daughter as mere payment;
  arbitrary dream, prophecy, or timeline devices used to solve continuity.

packages.prompt_text:
# Prompt contract

## Verbatim writing prompt

> [WP] There is a city that is architecturally colorful. It is divided by districts, and each district has its own style, like Gothic, Chinese, Egyptian, Greek, steampunk, cyberpunk, biopunk, dieselpunk, raypunk, solarpunk, and more.
>
> Notes: The story should focus on the city architecturally not the people or culture;

## Story controls

- Working title: The City of Eleven Foundations
- Target length: 3,000–3,800 words
- POV: Third-person omniscient with city-scale, architectural focalization
- Tense: Past
- Tone and genre: Lyrical speculative architectural fantasy with civic suspense
- Audience/content rating: General audience / PG
- Required elements: A visibly colorful city divided into architecturally distinct
  districts; Gothic, Chinese, Egyptian, Greek, steampunk, cyberpunk, biopunk,
  dieselpunk, raypunk, and solarpunk design languages; at least one additional
  architectural district; material, structural, spatial, and infrastructural
  detail; a complete dramatic change whose cause and resolution are expressed
  through the built environment.
- Prohibited elements: Named humanoid protagonists; people or culture becoming
  the emotional or thematic center; ethnic caricature or flattening a living
  architectural tradition into costume; a static travelogue with no causal
  arc; unexplained contradiction of established shared-universe canon.

## Assumptions

- The prompt's architectural focus permits people to appear only as anonymous
  traces of scale, occupancy, maintenance, evacuation, and return.
- "Chinese" is interpreted through specific architectural techniques—such as
  timber frames, dougong brackets, courtyards, screens, roof profiles, and
  glazed tile—rather than through generalized cultural decoration.
- The city is a local, story-scale invention in an unspecified place and era
  unless canon research establishes a suitable setting.
- The eleven design languages form genuinely different structural and
  infrastructural systems, not merely differently decorated façades.
- The central dramatic question concerns whether the divided built systems can
  survive a citywide physical crisis without erasing their distinctions.

## Completion tests

- The result is a complete short story, not a synopsis or chapter fragment.
- The central promise of an architecturally colorful district-city is
  dramatized through at least eleven legible architectural systems and resolved
  through a physical transformation of the city.
- Architecture—not an individual or a culture—remains the story's primary
  subject in every major scene.
- The story avoids an inventory-like tour by giving changes in one district
  consequences for at least three others.
- The Chinese architectural district is rendered in material and structural
  terms without stereotype.
- The story passes canon and continuity review.
- Every character-facing name and alias is checked against `stories/NAMES.md`;
  any deliberate reuse has a documented narrative reason.

packages.prompt_text:
# Prompt contract

## Verbatim writing prompt

> **[WP] "So if you win the duel, you get to take her on a date." They both nodded. "And if she wins the duel, she gets to take you on a date." They both nodded. "So why don't you both just... Skip that and go on a date?" They both glared.**

## Story controls

- Working title: The Courtesy of Blades
- Target length: 2,500–4,000 words, aiming near 3,300
- POV: Close third person, centered on one of the duelists; brief shifts are
  permitted only if they materially improve the romantic resolution
- Tense: Past
- Tone and genre: Warm fantasy romantic comedy with sincere emotional stakes,
  competitive banter, and a brisk action climax
- Audience/content rating: Teen; non-graphic fantasy violence, no sexual content
- Required elements: The prompt's complete exchange must appear in substance;
  two mutually interested people insist on a duel whose winner earns the right
  to take the other on a date; both glare when told to skip it; the duel must
  expose the emotional or cultural reason neither can simply ask; the woman is
  an active, skilled participant with an independent goal; the contest is
  nonlethal and meaningfully affects the relationship; the story ends with a
  freely chosen date or its unmistakable beginning
- Prohibited elements: Treating either person as property or a passive prize;
  coercive romance; a lethal outcome; sexual violence; resolving the premise
  as only a one-note joke; contradicting authoritative universe canon; quietly
  promoting proposed inventions into canon

## Assumptions

- The duelists are adults and already attracted to one another.
- The quoted speaker is a frustrated friend, official, or second who recognizes
  the obvious mutual interest but initially misses what the ritual means to the
  duelists.
- The duel is governed by safety rules and may be interrupted by a local,
  story-scale complication that forces cooperation without erasing the need for
  an honest romantic choice.
- The setting may use a canon-compatible pocket of the shared fantasy universe;
  any culture, location, custom, or rule not established in `universe/` will be
  labeled as a proposed invention.
- No character-facing name will be reused merely for convenience.

## Completion tests

- The result is a complete 2,500–4,000 word short story, not a synopsis or
  chapter fragment.
- The central promise is dramatized on page: the duel, the quoted logical
  objection, the mutual glare, and the eventual date all receive payoff.
- The duelists' apparently irrational insistence becomes emotionally coherent
  while remaining funny.
- Both leads demonstrate agency, competence, vulnerability, and affirmative
  consent; neither is reduced to a prize.
- The ending resolves both who wins (or how the contest is validly concluded)
  and whether they choose one another.
- The story passes both required canon and continuity review gates with no
  unresolved Critical or Major findings.
- Every reusable invention is recorded in `06-canon-delta.md` as a proposal,
  not established canon.
- Every character-facing name and alias is checked against `stories/NAMES.md`;
  any deliberate reuse has a documented narrative reason.

packages.prompt_text:
# Prompt contract

## Verbatim writing prompt

> **[WP] You did it. You did what was thought to be impossible and broke the prophecy. But as you stare at the cost, you begin to wonder if was even worth it to break the prophecy.**

## Story controls

- Working title: The Future That Refused Us
- Target length: 2,500–4,000 words
- POV: Close third person, limited to the person who breaks the prophecy
- Tense: Past
- Tone and genre: Dark mythic fantasy; intimate, morally complicated, and ultimately humane
- Audience/content rating: Mature teen / PG-13; aftermath of violence and grief without graphic gore
- Required elements: A prophecy that is genuinely binding; an apparently impossible and intentional breach; a concrete, visible cost caused by that breach; a protagonist who helped choose the cost rather than merely discovering it; a sincere reckoning with whether freedom was worth the casualties; an ending that resolves the protagonist's next moral choice
- Prohibited elements: The prophecy merely being false, mistranslated, or satisfied through wordplay; an abstract or entirely off-page cost; a reset that erases the consequences; a purely triumphant ending; nihilism that makes the original choice meaningless by default

## Assumptions

- The story stands alone while remaining compatible with the shared universe.
- Breaking the prophecy frees people from a predetermined future, but the institutions and protections built around foreknowledge cannot survive unchanged.
- The cost follows causally from both the method of breaking the prophecy and the sudden loss of certainty.
- The ending may remain morally ambiguous, but the protagonist must make a concrete choice about responsibility in the newly unwritten future.

## Completion tests

- The result is a complete short story, not a synopsis or chapter fragment.
- The central promise of the prompt is dramatized and resolved.
- The prophecy is shown to have been real and is broken rather than evaded.
- The cost is personal, societal, visible in-scene, and traceable to the protagonist's choice.
- The protagonist confronts a credible argument that preserving the prophecy would have prevented the present losses.
- The ending answers what the protagonist will do with freedom after victory, without undoing the breach.
- The story passes canon and continuity review.
- Every character-facing name and alias is checked against `stories/NAMES.md`;
  any deliberate reuse has a documented narrative reason.

# Prompt contract

## Verbatim writing prompt

> **[WP] Every single noble family in your kingdom has an alliance with a dragon that watches over them. The royal family's dragon, despite being the biggest and scariest by appearance, is a total sweetheart.**

## Story controls

- Working title: The Gentlest Terror

- POV: Close third person, centered on a royal-family protagonist whose public

- Tense: Past.
- Tone and genre: Warm court fantasy with political tension, dry humor, and an
  earned hopeful ending.
- Audience/content rating: Teen / PG-13; non-graphic peril and intimidation,
  with no explicit sexual content or graphic violence.
- Required elements:
  - Every noble family in the kingdom has a meaningful reciprocal alliance with
    a dragon that watches over it.
  - The royal dragon is visibly the largest and most frightening dragon in the
    kingdom.
  - The royal dragon is genuinely and consistently a sweetheart, demonstrated
    through consequential choices rather than asserted as a joke.
  - The contrast between terrifying appearance and gentle character drives the
    central conflict and its resolution.
  - Dragons retain agency and are allies, not pets, heraldic ornaments, or
    weapons owned by human houses.
- Prohibited elements:
  - No reversal in which the royal dragon is secretly cruel, predatory, or
    manipulating the family.
  - No ending that depends only on other characters learning not to judge by
    appearances; the protagonist and dragon must make a costly, causal choice.
  - No contradiction of authoritative shared-universe canon.

## Assumptions

- The prompt establishes a particular kingdom and its noble-dragon alliance
  custom; where existing canon is silent, these remain local proposed
  inventions rather than universal facts about all dragons or governments.
- The royal family includes at least one person who knows the dragon's gentle
  habits intimately but must confront a court that values its terrifying image.
- Humor will arise from character and contrast without making the dragon
  childish, incompetent, or merely cute.
- The story will stand alone for a reader with no prior knowledge of the shared
  universe.

## Completion tests

- The result is a complete short story, not a synopsis or chapter fragment.
- The central promise of the prompt is dramatized and resolved.
- The story passes canon and continuity review.
- Every character-facing name and alias is checked against `stories/NAMES.md`;

# Prompt contract

## Verbatim writing prompt

> **[WP] You are a legendary blacksmith, sought out for your ability to fix anything. Talking swords, obsidian breastplates, staves made of crystal, daggers forged from dragon scales, you've done it all. The real challenge today is a young hero asking you to fix what they call their 'plot armor'.**

## Story controls

- Working title: The Last Thing I Could Fix
- Target length: 2,500–4,000 words
- POV: First person, from the legendary blacksmith's perspective
- Tense: Past
- Tone and genre: Wry, humane fantasy with an adventurous climax and a sincere emotional core
- Audience/content rating: Teen / PG-13; fantasy peril and non-graphic injury
- Required elements: A legendary blacksmith whose established repair work includes talking swords, obsidian armor, crystal staves, and dragon-scale daggers; a young hero who explicitly calls the damaged object or condition "plot armor"; a concrete diagnostic and repair process; escalating consequences that test the repair; a resolved central choice about survival, heroism, and personal agency
- Prohibited elements: A story that remains only a joke or sketch; effortless invulnerability as the solution; an unexplained authorial rescue; graphic gore; an unresolved ending; inventions presented as established shared-universe canon without evidence

## Assumptions

- "Plot armor" can manifest as a real, repairable magical protection inside the story world, but its operation must have observable rules, costs, and consequences.
- The blacksmith is famous but local and mortal; their skill does not establish a new universal law of magic.
- The young hero is old enough to choose dangerous work but young enough that adults' expectations have helped define the role for them.
- The smith's greatest challenge is ethical as well as technical: repairing protection must not mean restoring the hero to consequence-free use by others.
- The story will favor earned causality and shared responsibility over destiny, while still delivering the prompt's playful metafictional premise.

## Completion tests

- The result is a complete short story, not a synopsis or chapter fragment.
- The central promise of the prompt is dramatized and resolved.
- The story passes canon and continuity review.
- Every character-facing name and alias is checked against `stories/NAMES.md`;
  any deliberate reuse has a documented narrative reason.
- The repair process changes how the plot armor works in a way the reader can understand before the climax tests it.
- The climax requires the young hero and the blacksmith to act rather than survive by coincidence.
- The ending answers whether the blacksmith truly fixed the plot armor and what that repair costs.

slug: "empire-within"

# Nobody Spends Her Name

By the time the runner bled through the second towel, Elspeth had been awake for seventy-six hours and somebody had learned to write with her hand.

She was twenty-three. The runner had been old enough to carry her on his shoulders when she was small, and he had spent his last strength crossing two hostile rooms to put the papers at her feet.

He lay between the desk and the locked door of her private room, one shoe gone, breath bubbling thinly in his throat. Rain shone on the boards beneath him. He had come in through the back stairs, past three men who were supposed to stop a dying man before he reached her chair. One of those men now stood outside with his nose against the wall. The other two had left their posts on an order carrying her name.

The driver kept pressure on the runner's belly. She was twice Elspeth's age, gray beginning at her temples, sleeves rolled above old burn scars. She looked up once and shook her head.

On the desk lay two folded orders and a police deployment notice. The orders carried Elspeth's authorization marks, the phrases her crews expected, even the blunt little diagonal she cut across a date when she was angry. One sent four men toward the older rival's daughter. The other sent another crew after his younger son. The police paper promised a public-safety operation six minutes after the murders were meant to begin.

Six minutes: enough time for both houses to answer in blood, not enough time for either to clear its rooms before armored police arrived to collect guns, records, and whichever survivors could still be bought.

The runner caught Elspeth's wrist. His nails were blue.

“Not yours,” he said.

“I know.”

His grip tightened as though she had misunderstood. “Said your voice—wouldn't count.”

His hand opened. The driver felt for a pulse anyway.

Elspeth read the first order again. The letters crawled out of line, then settled. Her eyes burned. Behind them, something small and black kept beating its wings.

“The teams,” she said.

“One car answered,” the driver said. “Already moving. Second won't pick up. We have a man following the first.”

“Get the lieutenant.”

He was brought in by his collar. Twenty-eight, broad through the chest, and so frightened his teeth clicked when he saw the runner. He had used Elspeth's desk all afternoon while she settled trouble on other floors. He knew where the blank orders were kept. He knew which drawer held the seals.

Elspeth struck him across the brow with her pistol. He went down on one knee. Blood threaded into his eye.

“Who opened my room?”

“Nobody.”

She hit him again, lower. “Try it without the lie.”

His phone began to ring. He flinched toward it, then stopped himself with both hands in sight.

The driver checked the screen. “First car.”

Elspeth held out her hand. The lieutenant gave her the phone. She put it on speaker.

“Turn around,” she said.

Road noise filled the answer. A grown man breathing through his nose. “We were told you might say that.”

She looked down at the lieutenant. “By my lieutenant?”

The man did not answer.

Elspeth's attention slipped. For two seconds she stared at the dead runner's bare foot and could not remember which killing she was stopping.

“Which target?” she asked.

“The daughter,” the driver said.

“Which target?” Elspeth said again, into the phone.

“The daughter. But the underboss said your voice doesn't count if you call direct. Said you'd been awake too long and someone might have you at gunpoint.”

The lieutenant wiped blood from his eyebrow. His breath went out of him all at once. “He told all the floor leads that yesterday. Called it a continuity rule.”

Elspeth looked at him. The underboss had built her authorization phrases years ago, when her feet had not reached the floor from the office chair. He had never needed her drawer. He had only needed everyone to believe he could speak for her when she was weak.

“Boss?” the man on the phone said.

The pistol grip had gone warm in her hand. “Turn the car.”

“I need to know which voice—”

“Mine. Turn it, or the car following you puts you in the road.”

Silence. Then the distant click of an indicator.

The driver listened to another phone. “They're coming back.”

Elspeth lowered her gun. The lieutenant stayed on his knee.

“Stand up,” she said. “Find the second team.”

He stood. No thanks. That helped.

* * *

The driver took the long sedan south through rain, one hand on the wheel and one pressed to an earpiece. The lieutenant sat beside her with a towel against his eyebrow. Elspeth rode in the rear, the orders flat across her knees and the dead runner's blood drying in the creases of her hand.

The underboss did not answer any of her calls.

The older rival answered on the first ring.

“My daughter is alive,” he said. His voice moved slowly. It made room for every word to become a precedent. “My son is not at home.”

“My first car turned back.”

“Then one of my children has not been murdered by you.”

“Bring your daughter to the old athletic club. Basement pool. Keep her where you can see her; my second car isn't answering. We'll come in the south doors.”

The driver looked at Elspeth in the mirror, then shook her head. “South doors give him the gallery.”

Elspeth heard only *give him* and almost snapped at her. Then the rest arrived.

“East service door, then,” she told the rival. “That one's ours.”

He was quiet long enough for the rain to fill the car. “You used that door last time.”

“So you'll check it.”

“I'll check all of them.”

He hung up.

The driver took the next corner hard. “Second team still dark. One of ours from the first car has a chest wound. The daughter's people put rounds through the back glass before it turned. He needs a room now, not after.”

“Bring him to the club.”

“He's leaking bad.”

“Then bring the man who knows how to keep him alive.”

The driver relayed it without arguing. In the front seat, the lieutenant called one number after another. Each time he said only, “Report,” listened, and ended the call. Older men had laughed when Elspeth first put him on a floor. They no longer laughed where she could hear it. Tonight he looked sick enough to be nineteen.

The ward captain answered on Elspeth's third attempt.

“I understand there may be heightened activity,” he said. “Any deployment in the district would be an independent response based upon credible indications of an imminent disturbance.”

“Come to the club.”

“That would create an appearance of coordination which, given the sensitivities—”

“Say it again.”

He started again from the beginning. Jurisdiction. Officer readiness. Unverified complaints from responsible residents. His words arrived ironed and folded, each one hiding the same dirty shirt.

Elspeth closed her eyes. The black wings beat behind them, and the second telling slid past her as the first had. “You have the paper I have.”

He stopped.

“Basement pool,” she said. “Before your operation starts. Otherwise every house you ever took money from gets a copy before the first shield reaches a door.”

“Threats against public servants are taken seriously.”

“Good.”

She ended the call.

The lieutenant twisted around. “Found the second car.”

“Where?”

“Two streets off the club. Front seats empty. Nobody's looked in the back yet.”

“Fuck.” The driver pressed harder on the accelerator.

* * *

The athletic club had been closed long enough for the foyer mirrors to wear gray skins. Below, the empty pool sank through the basement like an opened grave. Rainwater had collected in the deep end. Broken lane markers hung from rusted hooks, and the painted depth numbers on the tile had flaked down to single digits.

Elspeth entered through the service door with the driver, the lieutenant, and four others. One of the others was carried between two men, his shirt black over the ribs. Nobody asked where to put him. They laid him near the locker-room wall, behind tile and concrete, and the driver knelt to hold him still while another man worked.

The older rival arrived across the pool deck with nine armed people and his daughter. The daughter looked older than Elspeth by perhaps five years. She wore a dark raincoat and held her pistol low, not hidden. Her father did not place her behind him. When one of his men tried, she stepped aside and the man let her.

The rival stopped beyond the diving board. His people watched Elspeth's hands, the doors, the gallery above. None watched her face for signs of childishness. That insult had been beaten out of them somewhere else.

“Where is my son?” he asked.

“Not with my people.”

“That's not an answer.”

“It's what I have.” Elspeth put the two orders and the deployment sheet on the wet tile. “A man bled out on my floor bringing me these. My marks. I didn't write them.”

His daughter looked down but did not approach. “Your car reached me.”

“It turned.”

“After it showed itself.”

“Yes.”

The rival looked at the papers on the tile and did not pick them up.

The ward captain came in with two plainclothes officers and irritation arranged on his face. He saw the rival's force, then Elspeth. The irritation thinned.

“This gathering is exactly the kind of escalatory event our planned visibility was intended to discourage.”

The rival's daughter gave a short, unbelieving laugh.

“Planned visibility,” the captain repeated, softer. “A limited intervention to ensure that any emerging conflict remains contained and does not migrate into residential areas.”

Elspeth pointed at the deployment sheet. “You sent that before there was a conflict.”

“I don't authenticate material in criminal possession.”

“Pull the raid and you keep your rank and your pension. You don't, the paper goes out and you're standing here when your men come through the doors.”

“Units already deployed operate at the discretion of the commander on scene. Any recall at this stage would require a documented change in circumstances, which I am not presently in a position to—”

“And you,” the rival said to Elspeth, as if the captain had stopped speaking. “If I walk out of here with no payment, every man who carries your seal learns two things. That my family can be hunted. And that afterward I will come to a meeting and talk.”

“Take payment from the man who spent my name.”

“Put him in front of me.”

A door opened in the gallery.

The underboss leaned over the rail. He had taken off his raincoat and rolled his cuffs neatly, as if he were about to carve a roast. Six of Elspeth's people stood behind him. Two kept their guns down. The others did not.

“There she is,” he said. “We have half the city awake, police moving, nineteen-year-olds in gun cars, and she's holding court in an empty pool.”

The lieutenant's hand moved toward his weapon.

“Don't,” Elspeth said.

The underboss smiled at the command as though she had performed a trick he taught her. “Give me the pistol, sweetheart. We can still bring this in.”

“Call off the second team.”

“Our people are here.”

“All of them?”

His eyes moved to the orders on the floor. “You found both letters. Good. Saves us pretending this can be repaired privately.”

The rival looked up at him. His people raised their weapons by degrees.

The ward captain stepped backward. “I am not party to an internal succession matter.”

“You don't need to be,” the underboss said. “Your operation begins on schedule. We settle the house and give you a quiet district by morning.”

The captain went completely still.

For a moment, every choice in the room showed its edge. The rival could kill everyone across the pool and call it family duty. The captain could let his approaching officers turn the basement into evidence and bodies. Elspeth's people could choose the man who had hired them, fed them, taught many of them the first rules—or the woman in front of the guns.

Then the lights died.

The first shot came from the dark behind the captain. It tore open one of the rival's men at the mouth. Teeth and blood struck the tile. The second shot broke the diving board. The daughter turned toward the gallery, and Elspeth saw the pale blink of a muzzle above her.

Elspeth hit her around the waist.

They went over the pool edge together. The daughter struck the sloped bottom on one hip. Elspeth landed across her and felt a bullet drag fire through the meat above her shoulder blade. Her face hit wet tile. Blood filled her mouth where she bit her tongue.

Gunfire rolled around the empty basin, concussive and directionless. Tile burst in white sprays. A man toppled into the shallow end and landed with his leg folded backward; his scream ended under the next volley.

“My father?” the daughter shouted.

Elspeth lifted her head. Shapes moved against the red emergency lights. The older rival had taken cover behind a pillar. He was firing toward the locker-room door, where two of the missing team had appeared among the captain's men.

“Alive.”

“You're hit.”

“Move.”

They crawled along the pool wall. The daughter dragged one leg. At the ladder recess she turned and fired twice, not at the loudest target but at the shape descending the steps. The shape fell forward, gun clattering into the deep end.

Above them the underboss shouted, “Hold your fire! We are not killing our own over her mistake.”

Some of his people obeyed. Some kept shooting. One man in the gallery lowered his weapon and stared at it, unable to decide which act would make him a traitor.

The driver appeared at the deep end, gray hair loose, one sleeve wet to the elbow with somebody else's blood. “Boss. Locker room's lost. We need the east door.”

“Take it.”

“Need two.”

Elspeth looked up. “Lieutenant.”

He had the ward captain on the floor behind the tiled bench. Blood covered half his face from where she had struck him, and more soaked his shirt at the side. He heard her the second time.

“Lieutenant!”

He glanced over.

“East door. With her.”

The driver shook her head. “He's opened up.”

“Can you move?” Elspeth called.

The lieutenant pressed his hand to his side and nodded once.

“Then go.”

He went. He left the captain down behind the bench and crossed through the shots bent almost double.

The daughter watched him. So did her father.

The captain clawed for his radio. “Units are entering.”

Elspeth pushed herself up the slope of the pool. Her left arm hung badly, but it moved. “Call them off.”

“The scene is active. Withdrawal would expose personnel to unmanaged risk.”

A plainclothes officer beside him took a round in the neck. He clapped both hands over the wound and made a wet, astonished noise. The captain stared as the blood slipped between the man's fingers.

“They come in,” Elspeth said, “they find you standing with him.” She nodded toward the gallery. “And one of yours dead from his gun.”

The captain looked at the underboss. The underboss's attention was on Elspeth's crew, his hands spread as if calming difficult relatives.

“Temporary hold,” the captain said into the radio. “All units maintain perimeter pending threat reassessment. Do not breach. Repeat, do not breach.”

The sirens outside reached the building and stopped there.

The gunfire thinned. The driver and lieutenant forced the east door open, and cold rain-air moved through the basement. Two of Elspeth's wounded crawled toward it. One of the underboss's men tried to block them. The driver shot him through the cheek; he fell choking against the wall, one eye working as his hands searched uselessly for the ruin of his face.

“Enough,” Elspeth said.

She climbed out of the pool with the rival's daughter braced against her good side. Her voice barely reached the gallery, but the shooting had thinned enough for everyone there to hear.

The underboss's people looked down at them. At the daughter Elspeth had pulled under the first shot. At the lieutenant bleeding beside an open door. At the underboss, clean behind the rail.

Elspeth pointed to the man who had frozen. “Put it down or use it.”

His gun hit the carpet.

Two others lowered theirs. One backed away from the rail. The remaining pair turned their weapons toward Elspeth.

The older rival fired. One vanished backward. The other shot first, striking Elspeth's wounded man by the wall, before the driver killed him.

The underboss's face lost its patient shape. He drew and fired at Elspeth. The rival's daughter shoved her aside; the shot broke tile between them. Then the underboss ran through the gallery door.

Elspeth went after him.

* * *

The machinery corridor smelled of rust, chlorine, and hot wiring. Pipes crowded the low ceiling. Somewhere ahead the emergency generator hammered unevenly, loud enough to blur footsteps.

The underboss waited beyond a bend, his back to the generator housing. His pistol hung beside his thigh.

“Look at you,” he said. “We kept you alive all those years so you could bleed out in a condemned basement.”

Elspeth leaned against the wall. The black wings behind her eyes had become a whole dark room. “You sent them.”

“We built the house. We made the arrangements. We paid for every mistake you called instinct.” His free hand opened toward her, paternal even now. “Come here. Give me the gun. The captain wants stability, the rival wants his children, our people want breakfast without a war. I can still give them that.”

“With me dead.”

“Gone. It didn't have to mean dead.”

She heard *had to mean dead*. “What?”

“I said it didn't have to mean that.”

The generator missed and caught again. Beneath it came a smaller sound: rubber dragging once on concrete behind the housing.

Elspeth almost folded it into the noise. Almost.

From the corridor behind her, the lieutenant gasped, “Left.”

A crouched man rose from behind the housing. Elspeth fired toward the movement. His shot went into the ceiling; hers opened his chest and threw him against the pipes. He slid down, trying to hold himself closed.

The underboss moved at the same time. His first bullet went through Elspeth's coat without finding her. She struck his gun arm aside, and he drove his forehead into her face. White light burst across her vision. He caught her wounded shoulder and squeezed until her legs failed.

“We could have saved this,” he said into her hair.

Elspeth put the pistol against the soft shelf beneath his jaw and fired.

The shot snapped his head back. Bone and blood struck the generator housing. He remained upright for a surprised second, hands opening and closing, then folded across her legs. A loose bubbling came from what remained of his throat.

She shoved him off and sat against the wall until the corridor stopped leaning.

The lieutenant came up beside her. His hand was still clamped to his side.

“You good?” he asked.

Elspeth looked at him.

“Stupid question,” he said. “Can you stand?”

“Yes.”

He offered his arm. She used the pipe instead.

* * *

Back at the pool, the older rival had his coat pressed against his daughter's leg. His surviving people held the deck. Elspeth's people held the doors. The arrangement could have become a war if anyone breathed wrong.

The rival looked past Elspeth at the blood on the lieutenant, then at the underboss's pistol in her hand.

“Finished?” he asked.

“He's dead.”

“My son?”

The driver checked her phone. “Back of the second car, two streets over. Down in the footwell under a coat. Scared. Not touched.”

The rival closed his eyes once. When he opened them, he looked at his daughter.

“She pulled me clear,” the daughter said. Her voice shook now that nobody was shooting. “She got hit doing it.”

Her father considered Elspeth across the ruined tile. Then he lifted two fingers. His people lowered their guns.

“This settles tonight,” he said. “Not the road your car took.”

“I know.”

He turned to his daughter and began giving slow instructions about the car, the doctor, her brother.

The ward captain stood carefully. Blood from his dead officer had reached the knees of his trousers. “The perimeter will remain while we conduct an orderly disengagement.”

Elspeth held out her hand.

He stared at it.

“Your radio.”

“That is official property.”

“Then use it. Cancel the raid.”

He glanced at the deployment paper, at the dead men belonging to both houses, at the underboss's surviving loyalists facedown by the gallery stairs. His next radio call contained provisional assessments, revised thresholds, and resource concerns. It took him ninety seconds to say the operation was over.

Outside, engines started. One by one, the police vehicles moved away without entering.

The driver pointed at the man who had dropped his gun. He was on his knees, staring at the bodies. “Him?”

Elspeth had to follow her finger twice before she understood.

“He froze,” Elspeth said. “He didn't turn.”

“And tomorrow?”

“He comes back without a gun.”

The driver nodded and gave the man a strip of cloth for somebody else's wound.

Elspeth surveyed what remained. Four active traitors lay dead. Two had surrendered. One had escaped through the kitchen and would keep running until fear or hunger made his next decision. Her runner was still back in her private room, cooling on the blood-soaked boards. The man with the chest wound had stopped breathing during the fight. The lieutenant sagged against the east door, upright only because the metal bar held him.

“Get the wounded into cars,” she said. “Then go back for the runner.”

The men on the doors moved, and the driver with them. The lieutenant moved first.

leave the date out of the it so we can move the story more feelly around the timelines.

this feels really like the story "Still Taking Runaways" and not enough like a BRITH OF SUPER POWERS story it should be... like EPIC...

it should highlight the huge array of different powers from the ones i listed to others standard or more interesting just if 40% of 7B get them that lot of craziness...

so i think focusing on one person is going to be a mistake; your going to need to think really hard about this one.

how are we handling the 2.7 Billion points of view on this choas?

that not enough points of view... i think we need a different way to write this type of story.

think doctor Xavier and cerebral how when show in tv and movies he just gets a small glimpse of the person based on the search conditionals this could be are focal personal that lets us quickly move around between people with no setup for that person needed and move on  just a quickly;

# User's connection to the prompt's ending

i think this new direction helps with the ending of prompt:

"1.3 billion dead or missing in the first 24 hours; No one know what happened or why but your starting to put the pieces together."

# Production direction

The user requests an epic birth-of-superpowers story, with a clear departure from the small theatrical and animated-object structure of Still Taking Runaways. Make the worldwide transformation and the emergence of powers the story's central action. Keep catastrophe and violence non-graphic, then classify the finished prose and cover under the collection's AO3 rating definitions. Omit the calendar date from the prose. The undated modern-looking setting has no asserted connection to an existing era or system; it does not place active magic in the Long Dark.

The fictional world's starting population is seven billion; forty percent means 2.8 billion people develop powers. Show a huge variety, including the user's familiar powers and inventive additional abilities, as pervasive lived disorder, wonder, exploitation, and rescue. Variety must affect the action and the surrounding world rather than appear solely as a list or a closing report.

All story action and the ending occur within the first twenty-four hours. There is no later scene or epilogue. Narration may state the prompt's first-day totals retrospectively without adding later action; do not give an eyewitness unexplained immediate access to a complete census. Powers are unfamiliar and people are improvising under pressure throughout the day.

The user has rejected a single person's adventure and the proposed five-recurring-viewpoint ensemble, then supplied a different form: a focal searching consciousness, like Xavier using Cerebro to glimpse people selected by changing conditions. Use that analogy to create an original power and person, with brief immediate access to many independent lives rather than lengthy setup for a small cast. The focal search must reveal the planetary birth and accumulate the partial discovery promised by the original ending. It does not need to converge everyone's action into one local crisis or make the focal person a universal coordinator. Preserve the epic birth, pervasive variety, unknown origin, partial discovery, and first-day limit together; do not replace the story with a catalogue of abilities, a search tutorial, or reports.

# Prompt contract

## Verbatim writing prompt

> **[WP] The benevolent monarchy people have long since come to worship is really just a dozen or so dragons in disguise, hoping to set up a state that can keep everything not on fire for a few hundred years so that they can finally get some actual quality slumber.**

## Revision directive

> i think you took the "Not on Fire" part too literal; rethink the prompt and
> try again.

## Story controls

- Working title: The Peace They Could Sleep Through
- Target length: 2,500–4,000 words
- POV: First person, from a human royal adjudicator whose professional faith in
  benevolent monarchy has helped make the state dependent on royal answers.
- Tense: Past.
- Tone and genre: Wry, humane political fantasy with institutional comedy,
  moral tension, and an earned hopeful ending.
- Audience/content rating: Teen / PG-13. Threatened civil conflict, religious
  pressure, deception, and non-graphic historical violence are acceptable.
- Required elements:
  - The revered monarchy is genuinely a disguised collective of roughly twelve
    dragons, not merely advised or controlled by them.
  - Their sincere practical motive is to build a state stable enough to avoid
    wars, coups, famine, collapse, and other civilization-scale emergencies
    while they sleep for several centuries.
  - Their rule has produced substantial real good even though their identities,
    genealogy, and ultimate motive are concealed.
  - Royal worship has become part of the problem: people have learned to await
    perfect judgments from above rather than own difficult compromises.
  - The secret must be revealed early enough to create the protagonist's main
    choice and must directly shape the climax.
  - Humans must avert an imminent political breakdown through negotiation,
    responsibility, and revisable institutions rather than a final royal
    decree; the dragons must accept uncertainty in order to sleep.
- Prohibited elements:
  - No literal fire, arson, dry cistern, firefighting, or burning-building
    crisis as the story's central engine.
  - Do not reuse the plot, cast, names, worship structure, civic institutions,
    or constitutional settlement from `a-crown-of-quiet-hours`.
  - No effortless dragon intervention, perfect ruler, simple “monarchy bad”

# Prompt contract

## Verbatim writing prompt

> **[WP] You are a child of a great mage lineage, your eldest sister could turn forests into ash with her flames, your older brother capable of freezing oceans over, your younger sibling, a tamer of magical beasts, but for some reason, everyone fears you the most, and you have zero clue why.**

## Story controls

- Working title: The Shape of Mercy
- Target length: 2,500–4,000 words
- POV: First-person, tightly limited to the feared sibling
- Tense: Past
- Tone and genre: Character-driven high fantasy; wry mystery that deepens into
  emotional and morally serious family drama
- Audience/content rating: Teen / PG-13; magical peril and non-graphic injury
- Required elements: A renowned mage lineage; an eldest sister whose fire can
  reduce forests to ash; an older brother able to freeze oceans; a younger
  sibling who tames magical beasts; a protagonist feared more than all three;
  the protagonist's sincere ignorance of the reason; a concrete, dramatized
  revelation; and a choice that resolves what the protagonist will do with the
  truth
- Prohibited elements: Treating the mystery as only a baseless
  misunderstanding; making the protagonist secretly omniscient; gratuitous
  cruelty; a lore dump in place of a climax; contradicting authoritative canon;
  or ending before the central revelation and choice

- The protagonist is the third of four siblings and is old enough to act
  independently but still shaped by the family hierarchy.
- The siblings' spectacular powers are real, though the short story may show
  their scale through consequences and credible threat rather than destroying
  an ocean or forest on-page.
- The family's fear has a real magical and emotional cause. The protagonist's
  ignorance is itself part of the causal mystery, not mere social obliviousness.
- The family can be frightened, loving, compromised, and wrong at the same
  time; no relative must become a one-note villain.
- Any setting additions remain local, limited, and explicitly proposed in
  `06-canon-delta.md` rather than treated as established universe facts.

- The result is a complete short story, not a synopsis or chapter fragment.
- The central promise of the prompt is dramatized and resolved.
- All three siblings' signature powers matter to the action or the
  protagonist's central choice.
- The reveal explains both why others are afraid and why the protagonist did

# Prompt contract

## Verbatim writing prompt

> [WP] A person dies and wakes up in a train station, one train leading to heaven and the other to hell, anyone who is meant for hell but trys to enter the train to heaven will get dragged to hell while on the train, not wanting to find out what the afterlife is like, they stay at the station

## Story controls

- Working title: The Station Between
- Target length: 2,500–4,000 words
- POV: First person, centered tightly on the dead protagonist.
- Tense: Past.
- Tone and genre: Literary dark fantasy with existential tension, restrained
  dread, and humane emotional stakes.
- Audience/content rating: PG-13; death, grief, fear of damnation, and implied
  supernatural punishment, without graphic torture or gore.
- Required elements:
  - The protagonist dies and awakens in a train station.
  - Two trains are understood to lead respectively to heaven and hell.
  - A person assigned to hell who boards the heaven train is dragged to hell
    during the journey.
  - The protagonist refuses to test either destination because they do not want
    to discover what the afterlife is like.
  - Remaining at the station is a sustained dramatic choice with consequences,
    not merely an opening image.
  - The ending resolves what staying means for this protagonist while preserving
    the prompt's core outcome that they stay at the station.
- Prohibited elements:
  - No silent replacement of the two-train premise with a different cosmology.
  - No graphic depiction of torture, bodily destruction, or the protagonist's
    death.
  - No effortless loophole that removes the moral and emotional cost of refusing
    both trains.
  - No canon promotion or edits to authoritative `universe/` notes without
    explicit user approval.

## Assumptions

- The station and its procedures will be treated as a local, story-scale
  afterlife manifestation unless the canon brief establishes broader rules.
- The protagonist may interact with attendants or other dead people, but the
  protagonist's final choice must remain central.
- “Meant for hell” describes the station's apparent assignment system; the
  story need not prove that system morally infallible unless canon requires it.
- The trains' destinations may remain partly mysterious so long as the danger
  of boarding the wrong train is concrete and the central dramatic question is
  answered.
- The protagonist can change emotionally without changing the promised physical
  outcome: at the end, they still remain at the station.

## Completion tests

- The result is a complete short story, not a synopsis or chapter fragment.
- The central promise of the prompt is dramatized and resolved.
- The story passes canon and continuity review.
- Every character-facing name and alias is checked against `stories/NAMES.md`;
  any deliberate reuse has a documented narrative reason.
- The polished story falls within 2,500–4,000 words.
- Both destination trains appear on the page, and the wrong-train consequence
  affects the protagonist's decision rather than serving as background trivia.

## Verbatim writing prompt

> **[WP] You're an apprentice at a prestigious magic school! It's time for you to take your flying assessment, and take to the skies. Others choose brooms, levitation spells, or mounts. You show up with something a little different.**

## Verbatim revision directive

## Verbatim peer-method revision directive

> i now like the end story but the levitation is too close the main character novel idea; i am find with having 2 brooms (shows its the standard) and a flying creature (showing its rare but well understood)

## Verbatim wind-rune revision directive

> i think the runes should work more like wind magic; so its less like walking/running and more like flying with rockets boots (think witch hat atelier).

## Story controls

- Working title: The Weight of Falling Up
- Target length: 2,500–4,000 words
- POV: First person, centered on the apprentice taking the assessment
- Tense: Past
- Tone and genre: Wonder-forward school fantasy with a nimble, wry voice, playful magical invention, genuine airborne peril, and an emotionally satisfying resolution
- Audience/content rating: PG / broad teen and adult readership; non-graphic peril
- Required elements: A prestigious magic school; an apprentice facing a consequential flying assessment; two peers visibly using brooms so broom flight reads as the ordinary standard; one peer using a flying creature that reads as uncommon but familiar and well understood by the school; the apprentice visibly drawing wind-channeling magic runes directly onto their shoes as their different means of flight; those paired runes vent directed magical wind from the shoes and propel the apprentice through sustained flight with a rocket-boot-like feel; substantial action in the sky; an earned assessment result and complete character arc
- Prohibited elements: No solid-air footholds, luminous steps, air staircase, or walking/running-on-air mechanism as the primary flight model; no levitation candidate, levitation spell, or levitation comparison in the final story; no substitution of pre-enchanted shoes for the required act of rune drawing; no flight method that is merely a disguised broom or conventional mount; no protagonist mount, living flight partner, windlace, directional plummet, tether rig, or apparatus-centric engineering solution; no unearned rescue or deus ex machina; no dense procedural explanation that overwhelms wonder or character; no reuse of either rejected version's characters, names, schools, plot beats, set pieces, or prose; no contradiction of authoritative shared-universe canon

## Assumptions

- The revision directive is controlling: drawing magic runes on shoes is the story's central creative seed, not a cosmetic detail.
- The peer-method revision directive overrides the original prompt's levitation example for this production version. The final story uses two broom candidates and one flying-creature candidate instead.
- The two broom users should make broom flight feel established and standard without implying that every culture uses it. The creature should be rare at Nine Eaves but covered by familiar assessment procedures rather than treated as mysterious or unprecedented.
- The wind-rune directive supersedes the earlier air-step interpretation. The shoes function as paired wind-thrust focuses: rune geometry shapes direction and output, while the living wearer supplies power, balance, and moment-to-moment control.
- “Rocket boots” is a motion reference, not a technological claim: the flight should feel propelled, continuous, and burst-driven, with visible wind jets and differential thrust rather than solid surfaces underfoot.
- The *Witch Hat Atelier* reference is treated only as high-level inspiration for elegant, visually legible drawn magic; the story must retain its own terminology, imagery, and prose.
- The apprentice must draw at least one consequential rune on-page, and the climax must depend on how the shoe-runes work, fail, change, or are redrawn.
- The prompt does not require an existing character, school, era, or location, so canon-compatible local inventions are permitted.
- Because the previous result was rejected without line-specific feedback, this attempt keeps only the original prompt, title, and new rune-shoes directive while rebuilding all other creative choices from scratch.
- New reusable setting facts remain proposals in `06-canon-delta.md` unless explicitly promoted by the user.

## Completion tests

- The result is a complete short story, not a synopsis or chapter fragment.
- The central promise of the prompt is dramatized and resolved.
- The story passes canon and continuity review.
- The apprentice draws magical runes directly on their shoes on-page, and those runes are the actual unconventional means of flight.
- Two broom candidates visibly establish broom flight as the local standard, while the flying creature is visibly rare but institutionally understood.
- The shoe-runes remain materially distinct from the standard broom method, the flying creature, and both rejected flight concepts.
- Flight is propelled by directed wind thrust from the shoes, not by walking or running on solidified air.
- Foot angle and unequal left/right thrust visibly control pitch, yaw, braking, and recovery; damage to one rune produces a specific asymmetric failure.
- The final story contains no levitation candidate, spell, or comparison.
- The aerial climax and assessment result arise causally from the established rune mechanics and the apprentice's choices.
- The prose foregrounds magic, character, and sensation rather than reading like a technical manual.
- The new story has no substantive creative dependence on either rejected version.

# Prompt contract

## Verbatim writing prompt

> [WP] You find a magical wig that, when worn, turns you into the exact oppose of who you are, with the wig changing to match the new personality. However, you don’t believe this… until you put it on.

## Story controls

- Working title: The Wrong Side of the Part
- Target length: 3,000–3,800 words
- POV: First person, anchored in the wearer’s perspective
- Tense: Past
- Tone and genre: Darkly comic contemporary fantasy with mounting emotional
  tension, tactile magic, and a humane ending
- Audience/content rating: Teen / PG-13; non-graphic peril and emotionally
  fraught family conflict
- Required elements: A found wig; explicit disbelief about its alleged magic;
  a voluntary first wearing; a dramatic inversion of the protagonist’s
  habitual personality; the wig visibly changing to suit that inversion; real
  consequences caused by the transformed personality; and a resolved choice
  about what the wearer does with both the wig and the traits it reveals
- Prohibited elements: An “it was all a dream” explanation; treating the
  change as only cosmetic; a consequence-free reset; a simple good-self versus
  evil-self binary; or contradicting established shared-universe canon

## Assumptions

- “Exact opposite” means a coherent inversion of the protagonist’s dominant
  habits, defenses, and self-conception rather than a logically impossible
  reversal of every preference and fact.
- The protagonist remains conscious enough to experience and later reckon with
  what the inverted personality does.
- The wig’s origin and operation may occupy canon’s documented safe-invention
  space, but the story will prefer a local anomaly over a new global magic
  system.
- The physical transformation of the wig will be unmistakable on the page and
  will track the new personality rather than merely changing color.
- No existing character or location is presumed to appear unless canon
  research supports the choice.

## Completion tests

- The result is a complete short story, not a synopsis or chapter fragment.
- The central promise of the prompt is dramatized and resolved.
- The protagonist begins as a clearly legible personality, disbelieves the
  wig’s claim, puts it on, and becomes a comparably legible opposite.
- The transformed wig reflects the inverted personality in cut, texture,
  movement, and presentation.
- The inversion forces an irreversible truth or decision, so removing the wig
  cannot simply restore the opening status quo.
- The ending answers whether a person can use disowned traits without

  transgender friend whose excitement is sincere and whose identity is never

  reveal; an honest apology; mutual curiosity with explicit boundaries; and a

- Working title: What I Hate Most
- Target length: 2,500–4,000 words
- POV: Close third person, centered on one of the two romantic rivals.
- Tense: Past.
- Tone and genre: Dark romantic fantasy with dangerous competence, charged
  banter, luminous nocturnal imagery, and a playful fighting/flirting ambiguity.
- Audience/content rating: Adult characters; suggestive and sensuous but
  non-explicit; violence may be intense but not graphically gory.
- Required elements: The quoted exchange appears naturally on page; two adult,
  magically powerful rivals whose contest is also courtship; dark-queen or
  night-sovereign energy; a concrete reason one character resents having to
  "share" the other; consent and agency that keep possessiveness from becoming
  dehumanization; a decisive emotional and plot resolution.
- Prohibited elements: No person treated as a prize without meaningful agency;
  no coercive romance presented as healthy; no copied Suno lyrics; no ending
  that stops at banter without resolving the underlying rivalry; no silent
  contradiction of shared-universe authority.

  that suggestive fighting/flirting context.

  research identifies an especially strong compatible connection.
